newsitem.title: USA: U.S. opposes Khmer Rouge role in politics.
newsitem.headline: U.S. opposes Khmer Rouge role in politics.

text.p: The United States on Wednesday plunged into Cambodia's unravelling political situation, declaring its opposition to a role in national politics for Khmer Rouge guerrillas.
With Cambodia facing turmoil and violence, U.S. Secretary of State Madeleine Albright was reported to be rethinking her plans to visit the country next week.

"Since this issue of the Khmer Rouge is so prevalent in this crisis, the United States would be gravely concerned if senior Khmer Rouge leaders were permitted to play a role in Cambodian national politics or permitted to retain administrative control over areas occupied by Khmer Rouge defectors," State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns said.
"That's an important statement about our own view of how the situation should proceed," he told a news briefing.

He spoke a day after heavy fighting broke out in the streets of the capital Phnom Penh between bodyguards loyal to the country's two feuding prime ministers, revealing a further deterioration in Cambodia's stability.
Two bodyguards from co-Premier Prince Norodom Ranariddh's FUNCINPEC party and one bodyguard from co-Premier Hun Sen's Cambodian People's Party (CPP) were killed.

Ties between the two premiers, who have led a coalition government since 1993 elections, have sunk to a new low over Ranariddh's attempt to strike a deal with senior Khmer Rouge leader Khieu Samphan and bolster his political position in the run-up to elections due next year.
Hun Sen has declared that all talks with the Khmer Rouge are illegal.
Burns urged all sides to act to end the violence and called on Cambodia's leaders to resolve their politcal differences peacefully.
He said Albright has not cancelled her plans but there are growing concerns about security in Cambodia and she and her advisers "have to decide whether it makes sense to proceed."
Albright had planned to visit Phnom Penh on June 27-29 as part of an Asian trip that included Vietnam and Hong Kong for the June 30 handover of the British colony to Chinese control.
"She has not made a decision to cancel the trip, but she's obviously going to have to look at this in the days ahead," Burns said.

The State Department issued a travel advisory telling Americans in Cambodia to "exercise increased caution, especially in crowds and to avoid politcal gatherings or demonstrations, in the vicinity of political party and military buildings or compounds and areas with a heavy presence of military and bodyguard units," including Norodom Boulevard.
It also warned Americans not to leave their homes after nightfall.

Burns said he could not confirm a radio report that reviled Khmer Rouge leader Pol Pot had surrendered to his former comrades but said: "We don't shed any tears for him. He's a mass murderer. He ought to be brought to justice and tried for his crimes, which is genocide ... We hope that the end has come for Pol Pot."
